claim: The retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) is a collection of neurons at the ventral medullary surface that are activated by increased CO2 or low pH.
source: A candidate element of this circuitry is the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN), a collection of neurons at the ventral medullary surface that are activated by increased CO2 or low pH and project to the respiratory rhythm generator.

claim: Photostimulation of RTN neurons entrains the respiratory rhythm.

claim: Serotonergic neurons in the medulla have been proposed to play a dominant role in the central CO2 response.
source: Two sites have been proposed to play a dominant role in the central CO2 response: serotonergic neurons in the medulla (Ray et al., 2011; Teran et al., 2014) and the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN), a loose collection of neurons located ventral and immediately caudal to the facial nucleus (Goridis et al., 2010; Guyenet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) has been proposed to play a dominant role in the central CO2 response.

claim: RTN is a loose collection of neurons located ventral and immediately caudal to the facial nucleus.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: RTN neurons are defined by their location, expression of Phox2b and Vglut2, and absence of markers for nearby motor and catecholaminergic neurons.
source: RTN neurons—defined by their location, by the expression of Phox2b and of the vesicular glutamate transporter-2 Vglut2 (also known as Slc17a6) and by the absence of markers for the nearby motor and catecholaminergic neurons—are vigorously activated by increases in CO2 (Mulkey et al., 2004; Onimaru et al., 2012b; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RTN neurons are vigorously activated by increases in CO2.
source: RTN neurons—defined by their location, by the expression of Phox2b and of the vesicular glutamate transporter-2 Vglut2 (also known as Slc17a6) and by the absence of markers for the nearby motor and catecholaminergic neurons—are vigorously activated by increases in CO2 (Mulkey et al., 2004; Onimaru et al., 2012b; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neurons with the molecular characteristics of RTN neurons are already present ventral of the facial nucleus in the late embryo.
source: Neurons with the molecular characteristics of RTN neurons are already present ventral of the facial nucleus in the late embryo.
evidence: This is supported by prior work and observations in the manuscript.

claim: Embryonic RTN neurons have endogenous bursting properties.
source: The embryonic RTN neurons, previously termed embryonic parafacial cells, were found to have endogenous bursting properties and to couple with and increase the frequency of the respiratory rhythm generating (Feldman et al., 2013) pre-Bötzinger complex (pre-BötC) (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Embryonic RTN neurons couple with and increase the frequency of the pre-Bötzinger complex.
source: The embryonic RTN neurons, previously termed embryonic parafacial cells, were found to have endogenous bursting properties and to couple with and increase the frequency of the respiratory rhythm generating (Feldman et al., 2013) pre-Bötzinger complex (pre-BötC) (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Impairment of RTN development or function correlates with a blunted response to hypercapnia or acidification.
source: Impairment of RTN development or function correlates with a blunted response to hypercapnia or acidification (Nattie and Li, 2002; Dubreuil et al., 2009; Marina et al., 2010; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011; Takakura et al., 2013, 2014), and mouse models of congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS), which phenocopy the blunted or absent chemoreflex of the patients (Weese-Mayer et al., 2010; Rossor et al., 2014), have an atrophic RTN (Dubreuil et al., 2008; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mouse models of CCHS phenocopy the blunted or absent chemoreflex of the patients.
source: Impairment of RTN development or function correlates with a blunted response to hypercapnia or acidification (Nattie and Li, 2002; Dubreuil et al., 2009; Marina et al., 2010; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011; Takakura et al., 2013, 2014), and mouse models of congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS), which phenocopy the blunted or absent chemoreflex of the patients (Weese-Mayer et al., 2010; Rossor et al., 2014), have an atrophic RTN (Dubreuil et al., 2008; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mouse models of CCHS have an atrophic RTN.
source: Impairment of RTN development or function correlates with a blunted response to hypercapnia or acidification (Nattie and Li, 2002; Dubreuil et al., 2009; Marina et al., 2010; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011; Takakura et al., 2013, 2014), and mouse models of congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS), which phenocopy the blunted or absent chemoreflex of the patients (Weese-Mayer et al., 2010; Rossor et al., 2014), have an atrophic RTN (Dubreuil et al., 2008; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011).

evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work indicating ongoing debate.

source: In a recent study, mutants with a damaged RTN displayed a normal CO2/pH sensitivity at embryonic stages in vitro (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The majority of Phox2b-expressing RTN neurons co-express the Atoh1 transcription factor in the embryo.
source: To target the Phox2b-expressing RTN neurons with utmost specificity, we exploited the fact that the majority of them belongs to the small set of neurons that co-express the Phox2b and Atoh1 transcription factors in the embryo (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Rose et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Invalidation of Atoh1 in Phox2b+ cells curtailed the response to acidification in embryonic brainstem preparations.
source: We found that invalidation of Atoh1 in Phox2b+ cells, of Phox2b in Atoh1+ cells or of glutamatergic transmission in Phox2b+/Atoh1+ cells curtailed the response to acidification in embryonic brainstem preparations and eliminated the CO2 response in newborn pups.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Other contributors to the chemoreflex must act via the RTN or in partnership with it.
source: Together our findings imply that the RTN neurons that express or have expressed Phox2b and Atoh1 are essential for the activation of breathing by increased CO2 or low pH, and that other contributors to the chemoreflex must act via the RTN or in partnership with it.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Phox2b+ RTN neurons are glutamatergic.
source: The Phox2b+ RTN neurons are glutamatergic (Bochorishvili et al., 2012) and express the glutamate transporter Vglut2 already at embryonic stages (Dubreuil et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Phox2b+ RTN neurons express the glutamate transporter Vglut2 already at embryonic stages.
source: The Phox2b+ RTN neurons are glutamatergic (Bochorishvili et al., 2012) and express the glutamate transporter Vglut2 already at embryonic stages (Dubreuil et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In Vglut2::ChR2-YFP transgenic embryos, cells co-expressing ChR2-YFP and Phox2b were concentrated at the medullary surface ventral to the ChR2-YFP-negative facial neurons.
source: In the transgenic embryos, cells co-expressing ChR2-YFP and Phox2b were concentrated at the medullary surface ventral to the ChR2-YFP-negative facial neurons, thus well accessible to light delivered from the ventral surface (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and Figure 1A-C.

claim: At E14.5, single light pulses applied to the RTN region systematically evoked a burst of action potentials in ChR2-YFP expressing cells.
source: At embryonic-day 14.5 (E14.5), single light pulses (473 nm, 70 ms, 1–5 mW/mm2) applied to the RTN region in brainstem preparations systematically evoked a burst of action potentials in ChR2-YFP expressing cells (n = 5) that resembled the spontaneous rhythmic bursts (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 1D.

claim: The latency from light stimulus onset to the first action potential of the burst response was 192 ± 12 ms.
source: A latency of 192 ± 12 ms (n = 51 stimulations in three cells) was measured from the time of onset of the light stimulus to that of the first action potential of the burst response suggesting the requirement of a still unknown, slow obligatory process for burst initiation in the RTN.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: The latency from light stimulus to burst response suggests the requirement of a still unknown, slow obligatory process for burst initiation in the RTN.
source: A latency of 192 ± 12 ms (n = 51 stimulations in three cells) was measured from the time of onset of the light stimulus to that of the first action potential of the burst response suggesting the requirement of a still unknown, slow obligatory process for burst initiation in the RTN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed latency.

claim: At E15.5, when the preBötC is coupled to the RTN oscillator and drives a respiratory-like motor outflow, single light pulses delivered to the medullary surface triggered motor bursts in the C4 phrenic nerve roots.
source: 1 day later, when the preBötC is coupled to the RTN oscillator and drives a respiratory-like motor outflow (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009), single light pulses (473 nm, 150 ms, 1–5 mW/mm2) delivered to the medullary surface triggered motor bursts in the C4 phrenic nerve roots (hereafter C4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to prior work.

claim: When light pulses were set to activate the RTN at about twice the frequency of the ongoing endogenous rhythm, the C4 motor bursts could be entrained to the stimuli.
source: When the light pulses were set to activate the RTN in a rhythmic manner at about twice the frequency of the ongoing endogenous rhythm, the C4 motor bursts could be entrained to the stimuli and followed the light-imposed rhythm (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 1E.

claim: C4 motor bursts could not be evoked when the preBötC excitability was depressed by DAMGO.
source: C4 motor bursts could not be evoked when the preBötC excitability was depressed by the μ-opiate agonist D-Ala2-N-Me-Phe4-Glycol5-enkephalin (DAMGO, 0.3 μM, n = 4 preparations) (Mellen et al., 2003) (Figure 1F) or its development impaired genetically in Dbx1 null mutants (Bouvier et al., 2010) (n = 5 preparations) (Figure 1G) indicating that the motor outputs require an intact preBötC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: C4 motor bursts could not be evoked when preBötC development was impaired genetically in Dbx1 null mutants.
source: C4 motor bursts could not be evoked when the preBötC excitability was depressed by the μ-opiate agonist D-Ala2-N-Me-Phe4-Glycol5-enkephalin (DAMGO, 0.3 μM, n = 4 preparations) (Mellen et al., 2003) (Figure 1F) or its development impaired genetically in Dbx1 null mutants (Bouvier et al., 2010) (n = 5 preparations) (Figure 1G) indicating that the motor outputs require an intact preBötC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: The motor outputs from RTN photostimulation require an intact preBötC.
source: C4 motor bursts could not be evoked when the preBötC excitability was depressed by the μ-opiate agonist D-Ala2-N-Me-Phe4-Glycol5-enkephalin (DAMGO, 0.3 μM, n = 4 preparations) (Mellen et al., 2003) (Figure 1F) or its development impaired genetically in Dbx1 null mutants (Bouvier et al., 2010) (n = 5 preparations) (Figure 1G) indicating that the motor outputs require an intact preBötC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Malfunction of the RTN will result in lack of entrainment of the preBötC and thus of the motor output and in a slowed-down C4 activity.
source: These data suggest that malfunction of the RTN will result in lack of entrainment of the preBötC and thus of the motor output and in a slowed-down C4 activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing RTN's role in entraining preBötC.

claim: Atoh1 null mutants do not establish a proper respiratory rhythm and die at birth of respiratory failure.
source: Atoh1 null mutants (hereafter Atoh1−/−) do not establish a proper respiratory rhythm and die at birth of respiratory failure (Rose et al., 2009b), but the development of the RTN and CO2 chemosensitivity have not been examined in these mutants.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: E14.5 Atoh1+/− brainstem preparations show rhythmically active RTN neurons that increase their bursting frequencies in response to acidification.
source: Consistent with our previous observations (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009) calcium imaging of E14.5 Atoh1+/− brainstem preparations shows rhythmically active RTN neurons that increase their bursting frequencies in response to acidification.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: Rhythmically active RTN neurons were absent in Atoh1−/− mutants and could not be revealed by low pH.
source: These cells were absent in the Atoh1−/− mutants and could not be revealed by low pH (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 2A,B.

claim: At E16.5, Atoh1−/− mutants displayed a slowed-down respiratory-like rhythm in the C4 nerve roots by an average of 56%.
source: At E16.5, the mutants displayed a slowed-down respiratory-like rhythm in the C4 nerve roots (by an average of 56%, p < 0.001, n = 11 and 8 for control and mutants, respectively) and a complete lack of response to acidification (p = 0.1) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 2C,D.

claim: At E16.5, Atoh1−/− mutants displayed a complete lack of response to acidification.
source: At E16.5, the mutants displayed a slowed-down respiratory-like rhythm in the C4 nerve roots (by an average of 56%, p < 0.001, n = 11 and 8 for control and mutants, respectively) and a complete lack of response to acidification (p = 0.1) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 2C,D.

claim: In E18.5 Atoh1−/− pups, respiratory patterns ranged from hardly any breathing movements to slow rhythmic breathing that were completely unresponsive to hypercapnia.
source: In the mutants, respiratory patterns ranged from hardly any breathing movements to slow rhythmic breathing that were completely unresponsive to hypercapnia (p = 0.96, n = 31 and 8 for control and mutants, respectively) (Figure 2G–I and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data, Figure 2G-I, and Table 1.

claim: Atoh1 is essential for the formation of a functional RTN.
source: Together, the results show that Atoh1 is essential for the formation of a functional RTN and for CO2 chemical drive to breathe before and at birth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Atoh1 is essential for CO2 chemical drive to breathe before and at birth.
source: Together, the results show that Atoh1 is essential for the formation of a functional RTN and for CO2 chemical drive to breathe before and at birth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: In Atoh1−/− embryos, most RTN precursors fail to migrate to the medullary surface and accumulate instead dorso-laterally of the facial nucleus.
source: In Atoh1−/− embryos, most RTN precursors, whether defined by expression of the Atoh1 locus and Phox2b or by co-expression of Lbx1 and Phox2b, fail to migrate to the medullary surface and accumulate instead dorso-laterally of the facial nucleus (Figure 3A–F,I), consistent with previous findings (Rose et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data, Figure 3A-F,I, and a citation to prior work.

claim: In Atoh1−/− mutants, 83 ± 1.5% of the Atoh1-expressing periVII cells were found at a dorsal location compared to 32 ± 4.1% in the controls.
source: In the mutants, 83 ± 1.5% of the Atoh1-expressing periVII cells were found at a dorsal location compared to 32 ± 4.1% in the controls (p < 0.001, n = 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The cells co-expressing the Atoh1 locus and Phox2b that surround the trigeminal motor nucleus are present in Atoh1−/− mutants at their normal location.
source: By contrast, the cells co-expressing the Atoh1 locus and Phox2b that surround the trigeminal motor nucleus are present in the mutants at their normal location (p = 0.33, n = 3) (Figure 3G,H,J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 3G,H,J.

claim: In the brainstem, Atoh1 is expressed in the rhombic lip progenitors and its early differentiating progeny and essential for their specification.
source: In the brainstem, Atoh1 is expressed in the rhombic lip progenitors and its early differentiating progeny and essential for their specification.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Atoh1 function.

claim: A second, independent site of Atoh1 expression is post-mitotic, in cells that co-express the Phox2b transcription factor and surround the trigeminal motor nucleus (periV neurons) and the facial nucleus (periVII neurons).
source: A second, independent site of Atoh1 expression is post-mitotic, in cells that co-express the Phox2b transcription factor and surround the trigeminal motor nucleus (hereafter periV neurons) and the facial nucleus (hereafter periVII neurons, which include a majority of the RTN neurons) (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Rose et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PeriVII neurons include a majority of the RTN neurons.
source: A second, independent site of Atoh1 expression is post-mitotic, in cells that co-express the Phox2b transcription factor and surround the trigeminal motor nucleus (hereafter periV neurons) and the facial nucleus (hereafter periVII neurons, which include a majority of the RTN neurons) (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Rose et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the E15.5 brainstem, co-expression of Phox2b and Atoh1 is restricted to periVII and periV neurons.
source: In the E15.5 brainstem, co-expression of Phox2b and Atoh1 is restricted to periVII and periV neurons (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Rose et al., 2009b) (and see below).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and data in the manuscript.

claim: PeriVII and periV neurons are the only cells in the brain with the transcriptional signature of co-expressing Phox2b and Atoh1.
source: They are the only cells in the brain with this transcriptional signature, since Phox2b and Atoh1 are absent from more rostral regions (Rose et al., 2009a; Hirsch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In mice harboring the P2b::FLPo and Atoh1FRTCre alleles, Cre recombinase will be active selectively in cells with a history of both Phox2b and Atoh1 expression.
source: In mice harboring the P2b::FLPo and Atoh1FRTCre alleles, Cre recombinase will thus be active selectively in cells with a history of both Phox2b and Atoh1 expression (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on the genetic design and Figure 4B.

claim: In triple transgenic P2b::FLPo;Atoh1FRTCre;TauGFPnLacZ embryos, brainstem expression of the TauGFPnLacZ reporter was specific for periV and periVII cells.
source: Indeed, in triple transgenic P2b::FLPo;Atoh1FRTCre;TauGFPnLacZ embryos, brainstem expression of the TauGFPnLacZ reporter was specific for periV and periVII cells (Figure 4C,D), verifying that these cells are the only ones with a history of Phox2b and Atoh1 expression (hereafter Phox2bon/Atoh1on cells).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 4C,D.

claim: PeriV and periVII cells are the only cells with a history of Phox2b and Atoh1 expression.
source: Indeed, in triple transgenic P2b::FLPo;Atoh1FRTCre;TauGFPnLacZ embryos, brainstem expression of the TauGFPnLacZ reporter was specific for periV and periVII cells (Figure 4C,D), verifying that these cells are the only ones with a history of Phox2b and Atoh1 expression (hereafter Phox2bon/Atoh1on cells).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The nearby catecholaminergic neurons lie outside the Phox2bon/Atoh1on intersectional population.
source: Importantly, the nearby catecholaminergic neurons, despite their expression of Phox2b, lie outside the Phox2bon/Atoh1on intersectional population and are thus excluded by our approach.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic strategy and expression patterns.

claim: In the embryo, the Atoh1-expressing cells in the vicinity of the facial nucleus represent 85% of RTN neurons as defined by Phox2b and Vglut2 expression and the absence of catecholaminergic and motoneuronal markers.
source: In the embryo, the Atoh1-expressing cells in the vicinity of the facial nucleus represent a large fraction of RTN neurons as defined by Phox2b and Vglut2 expression and the absence of catecholaminergic and motoneuronal markers (85%, Dubreuil et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In P2b::FLPo;Atoh1FRTCre;R26tdTomato embryos, the tdTomato+ cells located ventral of the facial nucleus co-expressed Phox2b but not the motoneuronal marker Islet1,2.
source: The tdTomato+ cells located ventral of the facial nucleus co-expressed Phox2b but not the motoneuronal marker Islet1,2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 5A.

claim: TdTomato+ cells in the RTN region increased in numbers between E14.5 and E18.5, probably because of the time required for full recombination by Cre recombinase expressed from the Atoh1 locus.
source: They increased in numbers between E14.5 and E18.5, probably because of the time required for full recombination by Cre recombinase expressed from the Atoh1 locus, which starts only at E12.5 (Dubreuil et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase and knowledge of Cre recombinase kinetics.

claim: All tdTomato+ cells in the RTN region analyzed (297/297 cells from 7 different preparations) were rhythmically active and responded to acidification by increasing their bursting frequencies.
source: We then used calcium imaging to show that all tdTomato+ cells in the RTN region analyzed (297/297 cells from 7 different preparations) were rhythmically active and responded to acidification by increasing their bursting frequencies (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 5B-D.

claim: The burst frequencies and responses to acidification of the tdTomato–positive cells in P2b::FLPo;Atoh1FRTCre;R26tdTomato embryos were identical to those of the global population of oscillating RTN neurons.
source: Importantly, the burst frequencies and responses to acidification of the tdTomato–positive cells in P2b::FLPo;Atoh1FRTCre;R26tdTomato embryos were identical to those of the global population of oscillating RTN neurons (p = 0.5 and 0.7, respectively) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 5C.

claim: In E14.5 hindbrain preparations, tdTomato+ cells recorded in the whole-cell configuration featured spontaneous rhythmic burst discharges of action potentials whose frequency increased at pH 7.2.
source: In E14.5 hindbrain preparations, tdTomato+ cells recorded in the whole-cell configuration (n = 4) featured spontaneous rhythmic burst discharges of action potentials whose frequency increased at pH 7.2 (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 5E,F.

claim: Spontaneous bursts in tdTomato+ cells appeared as all-or-none voltage-dependent events that could be initiated by depolarizing current pulses.
source: These spontaneous bursts appeared as all-or-none voltage-dependent events that could be initiated by depolarizing current pulses (data not shown) and forced to terminate prematurely by negative current pulses (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 5G.

claim: Spontaneous bursts in tdTomato+ cells could be forced to terminate prematurely by negative current pulses.
source: These spontaneous bursts appeared as all-or-none voltage-dependent events that could be initiated by depolarizing current pulses (data not shown) and forced to terminate prematurely by negative current pulses (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 5G.

claim: The Phox2bon/Atoh1on cells share the functional signature of embryonic RTN neurons: they oscillate spontaneously and accelerate their rhythm in low pH.
source: Together, these data show that the Phox2bon/Atoh1on cells share the functional signature of embryonic RTN neurons: they oscillate spontaneously and accelerate their rhythm in low pH (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009) and thus are part of the intrinsically rhythmic network of embryonic RTN cells characterized by Thoby-Brisson et al. (2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: Phox2bon/Atoh1on cells are part of the intrinsically rhythmic network of embryonic RTN cells.
source: Together, these data show that the Phox2bon/Atoh1on cells share the functional signature of embryonic RTN neurons: they oscillate spontaneously and accelerate their rhythm in low pH (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009) and thus are part of the intrinsically rhythmic network of embryonic RTN cells characterized by Thoby-Brisson et al. (2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: In P2b::FLPo;Atoh1FRTCre;Ai32 embryos, single light pulses delivered to the RTN region in E15.5 brainstem-spinal cord preparations triggered a motor burst response in C4 and facial neurons in around 70% of the cases.
source: Single light pulses of 150 ms duration, delivered to the RTN region in E15.5 brainstem-spinal cord preparations at a fixed delay of 4 s after a spontaneous C4 burst, triggered a motor burst response in C4 and facial neurons (Figure 5H) in around 70% of the cases (130 out of 188 stimulations from 4 preparations).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 5H.

claim: The parameters of spontaneous and evoked C4 bursts in P2b::FLPo;Atoh1FRTCre;Ai32 embryos were not significantly different.
source: The parameters of spontaneous and evoked bursts measured on 150 spontaneous and 123 evoked C4 bursts, respectively, were not significantly different (spontaneous vs evoked: amplitude: 201 ± 152 arbitrary units (a.u.) vs 183 ± 117 a.u., p = 0.08; time to peak: 228 ± 17 ms vs 242 ± 14 ms, p = 0.53; half-width: 450 ± 21 ms vs 442 ± 17 ms, p = 0.76; decay time: 510 ± 25 ms vs 519 ± 22 ms, p = 0.79).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The latency of the C4 response to photostimulation and its variability probably reflect the delays caused by processes necessary for burst initiation in the RTN and in the preBötC.
source: The latency of the C4 response and its variability (666 ± 20 ms for 123 photostimulations), which cannot be easily explained by the time required for polysynaptic propagation of activity, probably reflect the delays caused by processes necessary for burst intitiation in the RTN (192 ± 12 ms, see above) and in the preBötC (Kam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed latencies and a citation to prior work.

claim: The Phox2bon/Atoh1on subset of RTN neurons is able to entrain phrenic nerve activity and thus inspiration.
source: Therefore, the Phox2bon/Atoh1on subset of RTN neurons is able to entrain phrenic nerve activity and thus inspiration as previously reported in adult rats of neurons in the RTN region defined by Phox2b expression alone (Abbott et al., 2009, 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: In experiments by Abbott et al., activation of breathing could not be unambiguously traced back to RTN neurons classically defined as non-catecholaminergic and non-cholinergic, since as many nearby catecholaminergic as non-catecholaminergic and some cholinergic neurons also expressed ChR2.
source: In the latter experiments, activation of breathing could not be unambiguously traced back to RTN neurons classically defined as non-catecholaminergic and non-cholinergic, since as many nearby catecholaminergic as non-catecholaminergic and some cholinergic neurons also expressed ChR2 (Abbott et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a critique of prior work supported by a citation.

claim: The RTN regulates inspiration, not only expiration.
source: Together, they show that the RTN regulates inspiration, not only expiration as postulated by others (Janczewski and Feldman, 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and contrasts with prior work.

claim: Opinions vary regarding the role of Phox2b-expressing RTN neurons in active expiration.
source: In fact, opinions vary regarding the role of Phox2b-expressing RTN neurons in active expiration.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: Abbott et al. found that activation of Phox2b+ cells in the RTN region also triggered active expiration.
source: Abbott et al. (2011) found that activation of Phox2b+ cells in the RTN region also triggered active expiration and Marina et al. (2010) that silencing these neurons in the in situ perfused brainstem-spinal cord preparation reduced hypercapnia-evoked expiratory activity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Marina et al. found that silencing Phox2b+ cells in the RTN region in the in situ perfused brainstem-spinal cord preparation reduced hypercapnia-evoked expiratory activity.
source: Abbott et al. (2011) found that activation of Phox2b+ cells in the RTN region also triggered active expiration and Marina et al. (2010) that silencing these neurons in the in situ perfused brainstem-spinal cord preparation reduced hypercapnia-evoked expiratory activity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Pagliardini et al. reported that photostimulation of cells expressing ChR2 from a pan-neuronal promoter in the RTN region generated mainly active expiration with little effect on inspiration.
source: By contrast, Pagliardini et al. (2011) reported that photostimulation of cells expressing ChR2 from a pan-neuronal promoter in the RTN region generated mainly active expiration with little effect on inspiration.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Pagliardini et al. attributed the effect seen in their experiments to neurons that did not express Phox2b.
source: These authors attributed the effect seen in their experiments to neurons that did not express Phox2b and are thus not targeted by our approach.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Tupal et al. reported that in E18.5 brainstem-spinal cord preparations, a lumbar motor output and thus active expiration persisted after the depletion of Atoh1 in RTN neurons.
source: Similarly, Tupal et al. (2014) reported that in E18.5 brainstem-spinal cord preparations, a lumbar motor output and thus active expiration persisted after the depletion of Atoh1 in RTN neurons.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A conditional genetic strategy that combines the criteria of Phox2b and Atoh1 expression will target periV in addition to periVII neurons.
source: A conditional genetic strategy that combines the criteria of Phox2b and Atoh1 expression will target periV in addition to periVII neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns.

claim: PeriV neurons are not essential to CO2 chemosensitivity.
source: We found that periV neurons are not essential to CO2 chemosensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: At E16.5, sectioning to remove the pons accelerated C4 discharges in baseline conditions by suppressing the inhibitory influence on the respiratory rhythm generator exerted by pontine neurons.
source: At E16.5, in baseline conditions, sectioning accelerated C4 discharges by suppressing the inhibitory influence on the respiratory rhythm generator (RRG) exerted by pontine neurons (Ito et al., 2000; Hilaire et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: The response to a pH challenge was fully preserved after sectioning to remove the pons.
source: However, the response to a pH challenge was fully preserved (Figure 6B,C) (p = 0.1, n = 34).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 6B,C.

claim: At least in vitro, periV neurons do not seem to contribute to the CO2/pH response.
source: Hence, at least in vitro, periV neurons do not seem to contribute to the CO2/pH response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Affecting periVII cells, but leaving periV neurons intact, suffices to eliminate the CO2 response.
source: Conversely, affecting periVII cells, but leaving periV neurons intact, suffices to eliminate the CO2 response: indeed, our previous results showed that conditional inactivation of Phox2b or activation of the toxic P2b27Alacki allele using Egr2Cre as Cre driver resulted in the lack of responsiveness to CO2 or acidification (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011), despite the fact that Egr2cre directs recombination in periVII (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011) but not in periV cells (Figure 6D–G).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and Figure 6D-G.

claim: Egr2cre directs recombination in periVII but not in periV cells.
source: Conversely, affecting periVII cells, but leaving periV neurons intact, suffices to eliminate the CO2 response: indeed, our previous results showed that conditional inactivation of Phox2b or activation of the toxic P2b27Alacki allele using Egr2Cre as Cre driver resulted in the lack of responsiveness to CO2 or acidification (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011), despite the fact that Egr2cre directs recombination in periVII (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011) but not in periV cells (Figure 6D–G).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and Figure 6D-G.

claim: In P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox embryos, Atoh1 expression was abrogated in the ventrolateral medulla at E15.5 and as early as E12.5.
source: Indeed, Atoh1 expression was abrogated in the ventrolateral medulla at E15.5 and as early as E12.5 (Figure 7B,C) attesting to an efficient recombination.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 7B,C.

claim: In P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox embryos, Atoh1 expression was preserved outside of the Phox2b lineages, that is, in the rhombic lip and the migrating cells of the anterior extramural stream.
source: Predictably, Atoh1 expression was preserved outside of the Phox2b lineages, that is, in the rhombic lip and the migrating cells of the anterior extramural stream.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: In P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox embryos, the normally Atoh1-expressing periVII cells were quantitatively preserved.
source: In P2b::CreBAC1; Atoh1lox/lox embryos, as in Atoh1−/− embryos, the normally Atoh1-expressing periVII cells that can be detected in these mutants by double Phox2b/Lbx1 labeling (Pagliardini et al., 2008; Rose et al., 2009b) were quantitatively preserved (p = 0.11).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: In P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox embryos, the distribution of periVII cells was massively shifted from ventral to dorsal.
source: However, their distribution was massively shifted from ventral to dorsal (75 ± 2.6% dorsally located Phox2b+/Lbx1+ cells in the mutants vs 25 ± 2.3% in the controls, p < 0.001, n = 3 and 4 for controls and mutants, respectively) and the ventral Phox2bon/Atoh1on RTN neurons correspondingly depleted, in agreement with previous results (Huang et al., 2012) (Figure 7D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data, Figure 7D-F, and a citation to prior work.

claim: In E14.5 P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mutant brainstem preparations, calcium activity in the RTN region showed few active cells, absence of synchronized rhythmic fluorescent changes and unresponsiveness to acidification.
source: In E14.5 brainstem preparations, calcium activity in the RTN region of the conditional mutants was similar to that observed in Atoh1−/− embryos: few active cells (8 ± 2 cells, n = 5 vs 119 ± 11 in the controls, n = 13), absence of synchronized rhythmic fluorescent changes and unresponsiveness to acidification (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 8A,B.

claim: At E16.5, the frequency of C4 discharges in P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mutants was reduced by an average of 49%.
source: At E16.5, the frequency of C4 discharges was reduced as in other mutants with impaired RTN function (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011) (by an average of 49%, p < 0.001, n = 12 and 15 for mutants and controls, respectively) (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data, Figure 8C,D, and citations to prior work.

claim: P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mutant preparations retained a residual response to a pH challenge, which was much attenuated.
source: The mutant preparations retained a residual response to a pH challenge, which, however, was much attenuated (an increase in C4 frequency by 51 ± 10% above the pH 7.4 value vs 106 ± 17% in the controls, p < 0.001, n = 12 and 15 for mutants and controls, respectively) and remained below the baseline value of the controls (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 8C,D.

claim: In E15.5 control preparations with Vglut2::ChR2-YFP, stimulation of the RTN region by single light pulses systematically elicited a synchronized calcium response in the RTN neurons, followed by a motor burst in the facial nucleus and the C4 roots.
source: In E15.5 control preparations, stimulation of the RTN region by single light pulses of 150 ms duration, delivered at a fixed delay of 4 s after a spontaneous burst (n = 147 photostimulations in 6 preparations), systematically elicited a synchronized calcium response in the RTN neurons, followed by a motor burst in the facial nucleus and the C4 roots (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 8E.

claim: In the P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox background with Vglut2::ChR2-YFP, light stimulus resulted in the activation of only a few RTN neurons and completely failed to trigger bursts in C4 and the facial nucleus.
source: In the P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox background, the same light stimulus resulted in the activation of only a few RTN neurons and completely failed to trigger bursts in C4 and the facial nucleus (n = 317 photostimulations in 6 preparations) (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 8F.

claim: The residual Phox2b and Lbx1 co-expressing RTN precursors that reach the medullary surface in P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mutants are unable to mount a motor response.
source: Therefore, the residual Phox2b and Lbx1 co-expressing RTN precursors that reach the medullary surface (see Figure 7F) are unable to mount a motor response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The dorsally misrouted periVII cells may underlie the residual chemoresponse in E16.5 P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox preparations.
source: Reasoning that the dorsally misrouted periVII cells may underlie the residual chemoresponse in E16.5 preparations, we compared the functional status of ventral and dorsal cells in E15.5 slice preparations (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis that motivated further experiments.

claim: In P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mutants, rhythmic cells were massively depleted ventrally, but a population of neurons with synchronized rhythmic activity was found dorso-laterally of the facial nucleus.
source: In the P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mutants, by contrast, rhythmic cells were massively depleted ventrally, but a population of neurons with synchronized rhythmic activity was now found dorso-laterally of the facial nucleus (n = 5) (Figure 9B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 9B,C.

claim: The dorsally located mutant periVII cells were functionally distinct from wild-type dorsal cells and resembled wild-type ventral cells.
source: The dorsally located mutant periVII cells were thus distinct from wild-type dorsal cells and functionally resembled wild-type ventral cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The ectopic periVII cells in the P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mutants accelerated their rhythm in low pH conditions.
source: The ectopic periVII cells in the P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mutants accelerated their rhythm in low pH conditions (Figure 9C,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 9C,E.

claim: The ectopic periVII cells in the P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mutants had conserved their glutamatergic nature.
source: They had conserved their glutamatergic nature (Figure 9F) and could thus mediate the attenuated C4 response to acidification in the brainstem-spinal cord preparations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 9F.

claim: The ectopic periVII cells in the P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mutants could mediate the attenuated C4 response to acidification in the brainstem-spinal cord preparations.
source: They had conserved their glutamatergic nature (Figure 9F) and could thus mediate the attenuated C4 response to acidification in the brainstem-spinal cord preparations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: In Atoh1−/− embryos, the dorso-laterally located rhythmic cells still responded to low pH but were fewer and less synchronized.
source: In Atoh1−/− embryos (n = 5), the dorso-laterally located rhythmic cells still responded to low pH but were fewer and less synchronized (Figure 9D,E), which may explain the complete absence of a response.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and Figure 9D,E.

claim: The fewer and less synchronized dorsal rhythmic cells in Atoh1−/− embryos may explain the complete absence of a response to acidification.
source: In Atoh1−/− embryos (n = 5), the dorso-laterally located rhythmic cells still responded to low pH but were fewer and less synchronized (Figure 9D,E), which may explain the complete absence of a response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: In newborn P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mutants at P0, mean ventilation in normal air was reduced by 16%.
source: In newborn mutants at the day of birth (P0), mean ventilation (VE) in normal air was reduced by 16%, (from 22.8 ± 0.3 to 19.2 ± 0.6 μl/s/g, p < 0.001, n = 13 and 31 for mutants and controls, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Hypercapnic air increased VE of the controls by 60 ± 13% but had no effect on P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mutants at P0.
source: Hypercapnic air increased VE of the controls by 60 ± 13% (p < 0.001) but had no effect on the mutants (p = 0.34) (Figure 10A and Table 1), and this was true also at P2.5 (Figure 10B–D) (p = 0.18, n = 9 and 17, for mutants and controls, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data, Figure 10A, and Table 1.

claim: Adult P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mutants breathing hypercapnic air responded with a 30% increase in VE, corresponding to an average of 42% recovery of the CO2 response with respect to the adult controls.
source: Adult mutants breathing hypercapnic air responded with a 30% increase in VE, corresponding to an average of 42% recovery of the CO2 response with respect to the adult controls (p < 0.001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The blunted CO2 response at later postnatal stages in P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mice is a recovery from an absent chemoreflex at birth.
source: Our results demonstrate that the blunted CO2 response at later postnatal stages in P2b::CreBAC1;Atoh1lox/lox mice is a recovery from an absent chemoreflex at birth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: A very similar recovery of the chemoreflex was found in adult Egr2Cre/+;Phox2b27Alacki/+ mutants.
source: We found a very similar recovery of the chemoreflex in adult Egr2Cre/+;Phox2b27Alacki/+ mutants (Ramanantsoa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The partial recovery of the CO2 response in adults could be due to late compensation by residual RTN neurons.
source: The partial recovery of the CO2 response in adults could be due to late compensation by residual RTN neurons, to a strengthening of peripheral chemoreceptor input that bypasses the RTN (Basting et al., 2015) or to some of the multiple sites proposed to function as CO2 sensors in the brain which would now also bypass the RTN (Nattie and Li, 2009).
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: The partial recovery of the CO2 response in adults could be due to a strengthening of peripheral chemoreceptor input that bypasses the RTN.
source: The partial recovery of the CO2 response in adults could be due to late compensation by residual RTN neurons, to a strengthening of peripheral chemoreceptor input that bypasses the RTN (Basting et al., 2015) or to some of the multiple sites proposed to function as CO2 sensors in the brain which would now also bypass the RTN (Nattie and Li, 2009).
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: The partial recovery of the CO2 response in adults could be due to some of the multiple sites proposed to function as CO2 sensors in the brain which would now also bypass the RTN.
source: The partial recovery of the CO2 response in adults could be due to late compensation by residual RTN neurons, to a strengthening of peripheral chemoreceptor input that bypasses the RTN (Basting et al., 2015) or to some of the multiple sites proposed to function as CO2 sensors in the brain which would now also bypass the RTN (Nattie and Li, 2009).
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: The lack of the chemoreflex in many human CCHS patients suggests that putative compensatory sites also have a history of Phox2b expression.
source: The lack of the chemoreflex in many human CCHS patients (Straus et al., 2010; Weese-Mayer et al., 2010) suggests that these putative compensatory sites also have a history of Phox2b expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the human data and supported by citations.

claim: The Phox2b+/Atoh1+ RTN neurons could be the main CO2 sensors in the brain.
source: Our findings are compatible with two explanations for the loss of the chemoreflex: the Phox2b+/Atoh1+ RTN neurons could be the main CO2 sensors in the brain or obligatory relays funneling the chemosensory input from other cells to the RRG—or both.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: The Phox2b+/Atoh1+ RTN neurons could be obligatory relays funneling the chemosensory input from other cells to the RRG.
source: Our findings are compatible with two explanations for the loss of the chemoreflex: the Phox2b+/Atoh1+ RTN neurons could be the main CO2 sensors in the brain or obligatory relays funneling the chemosensory input from other cells to the RRG—or both.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: RTN neurons are exquisitely sensitive to small changes in CO2/pH.
source: On the one hand, RTN neurons are exquisitely sensitive to small changes in CO2/pH (Mulkey et al., 2004; Onimaru et al., 2008), also when synaptically isolated (Wang et al., 2013) and, in close apposition to numerous capillaries (Onimaru et al., 2012a), well positioned to sense PCO2 in the blood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RTN neurons are sensitive to CO2/pH when synaptically isolated.
source: On the one hand, RTN neurons are exquisitely sensitive to small changes in CO2/pH (Mulkey et al., 2004; Onimaru et al., 2008), also when synaptically isolated (Wang et al., 2013) and, in close apposition to numerous capillaries (Onimaru et al., 2012a), well positioned to sense PCO2 in the blood.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RTN neurons are in close apposition to numerous capillaries and well positioned to sense PCO2 in the blood.
source: On the one hand, RTN neurons are exquisitely sensitive to small changes in CO2/pH (Mulkey et al., 2004; Onimaru et al., 2008), also when synaptically isolated (Wang et al., 2013) and, in close apposition to numerous capillaries (Onimaru et al., 2012a), well positioned to sense PCO2 in the blood.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RTN neurons receive afferences from many brainstem sites that contain putative chemosensors.
source: On the other, they receive afferences from many brainstem sites that contain putative chemosensors (Rosin et al., 2006) and respond with depolarization to activation of nearby acid-sensitive astrocytes (Gourine et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RTN neurons respond with depolarization to activation of nearby acid-sensitive astrocytes.
source: On the other, they receive afferences from many brainstem sites that contain putative chemosensors (Rosin et al., 2006) and respond with depolarization to activation of nearby acid-sensitive astrocytes (Gourine et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RTN neurons receive excitatory connections from the carotid bodies via the nucleus of the solitary tract.
source: In addition, RTN neurons receive excitatory connections from the carotid bodies via the nucleus of the solitary tract and increase their firing rates in response to carotid body stimulation by hypoxia (Takakura et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RTN neurons increase their firing rates in response to carotid body stimulation by hypoxia.
source: In addition, RTN neurons receive excitatory connections from the carotid bodies via the nucleus of the solitary tract and increase their firing rates in response to carotid body stimulation by hypoxia (Takakura et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The carotid bodies are the main PO2 sensors.
source: The carotid bodies are not only the main PO2 sensors, but provide also a substantial fraction of the overall CO2 response (Forster et al., 2000; Smith et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and is established knowledge.

claim: The carotid bodies provide a substantial fraction of the overall CO2 response.
source: The carotid bodies are not only the main PO2 sensors, but provide also a substantial fraction of the overall CO2 response (Forster et al., 2000; Smith et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the perinatal period, the RTN is an obligatory relay for all forms of respiratory chemoreception whether mediated by central or peripheral chemoreceptors.
source: The implication is that in the perinatal period, the RTN is an obligatory relay for all forms of respiratory chemoreception whether mediated by central or peripheral chemoreceptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing complete loss of chemoreflex in neonates.

claim: The RTN has been suggested to be a crucial hub for respiratory chemoreception because of its extensive connections with other chemosensory sites and the observation that its stimulation activates breathing.
